adaptations.strategy: One booklet for the whole school, graded lines. The 270 questions in questions.json are the script for every pupil from the first night of Year 8, and the booklet a Year 12 carries into the speaking exam is the same file a Year 8 opened four years earlier, with the early lines crossed through and dated above the later ones (the Líne screen already keeps drafts crossed through and dated, so no new structure is needed for this). What is graded is the line, not the booklet: a Year 8 line is one sentence in the present tense built from the frequency list (Tá deartháir amháin agam); a Year 10 line is two sentences, the second opening with a reason word from the list's multi-word phrases (mar, mar gheall ar, cionn is); a Year 12 line is a full answer with an opinion frame and a reason, as the brief already describes. The candidate box's third cell carries a real date the department sets for every year, not only the GCSE sitting: Comhrá, Meitheamh 2027 for Years 8 to 10 (the end-of-year conversation with a fluent speaker that the framework requires anyway) and Scrúdú, Bealtaine 2027 or 2028 for Years 11 and 12. Where the strategy strains, and it does, is in the data: of the 270 questions, 106 can be answered in one present-tense sentence by a beginner, 44 are shaped around a reason or an opinion, 42 carry the past tense, and about 30 (TGMO subjects, Ardléibhéal, BTEC, taithí oibre, Bliain a Sé, measúnú rialaithe) are meaningless to a 12-year-old. So the same 270 cannot be printed on a Year 8's rules unchanged; each question needs a tier (the brief already lists tier as a field to add), and a Year 8's sheet prints only tier 1 questions on its rules with the others in grey print further down the page, still present, not yet asked. The second strain is vocabulary: the KS3 list is a general frequency list, not a topic list, and it lacks deirfiúr, mamaí, daidí, guthán, éide, gorm, glas, suimiúil, greannmhar, dúil, is fearr and taitin, so roughly one Year 8 line in three will need a word the primary spine does not carry; the GCSE topic list carries most of them (deirfiúr, éide scoile, gorm, suimiúil, leadránach, greannmhar, guthán) but without gender, so the index recognises them and the pen does not judge their mutation. That is exactly the split the brief already makes for Years 11 and 12, so it holds. The third strain is honest: a script cannot supply the fluent speaker, and nothing in print can teach sound-symbol correspondences; the end-of-year conversation and Abair do those.
adaptations.threadForYear8: For a Year 8 the script is the same object the Year 12 holds: one booklet in her own name, two pages the department has fixed for the year (Mé féin agus mo theaghlach, An scoil), each cut into sheets of ten lines, and on every rule one of the examiner's own questions, printed, with the simplest ones (Cad é an t-ainm atá ort? Cá bhfuil tú i do chónaí? Cá mhéad deartháir atá agat?) on the first sheet and the harder ones in grey print at the foot of the page where she can see they are coming. What fills is the sheet: ten lines in biro, each one sentence in her own words, and when the tenth is written the hand writes Críochnaithe across it and the foot offers Priontáil an leathanach so her teacher gets a page with a tick box beside each line. The candidate box does not say Scrúdú and does not say an exam year she cannot picture; it says Comhrá, Meitheamh 2027, the afternoon at the end of Year 8 when she will sit with a fluent speaker (her teacher, or a visitor the department brings in) who will ask her these questions and nothing else, holding the page she printed. A 12-year-old opens it tomorrow because tonight the pen wrote her name on the cover and one kind line about one thing (fada ar 'Tá', maith thú), because tomorrow is one new line and one she already knows, five minutes, and because the booklet is hers: the only Irish in it is Irish she wrote, and by June there will be nothing the speaker can ask her that she has not already said.
adaptations.firstNightYear8: The inside cover first, filled as a candidate fills a real one. Ainm: Cara Ní Bhriain. Rang: 8C (the class field takes 8 to 12, not 11 or 12 only). Two pages: for Year 8 the two pages come ticked by the department (Mé féin agus mo theaghlach; An scoil) and the other ten sit in grey; she does not choose. Baile fearainn: An Sruthán, and as said after Tá mé i mo chónaí: sa tSruthán (the locative string fills Q002 and Q087 before display, as the brief already does for Q104 and Q105). Club: Imrím le CLG an tSrutháin, or left blank. The permanent cover text stands as written in the brief, with one sentence changed for Years 8 to 10: Faoi lá an chomhrá ní bheidh rud ar bith le rá agat den chéad uair. Then sheet 1a shown blank with its ten questions printed on the rules: Q001, Q002, Q003, Q004, Q005, Q006, Q007, Q009, Q010, Q011, the object before the paragraph. Then Anocht with one item, as the brief already specifies for every first night: the seven one-sentence questions Q001 to Q007, each on its own rule, marked together. What Cara writes, and what the pen does, line by line: Q001 Cad é an t-ainm atá ort? Cara is ainm dom. (pen: nothing; if she types Cara is ainm dom without the fada she would not, there is none to miss; if she writes Ta, fada! beside it.) Q002 Cá bhfuil tú i do chónaí? Tá mé i mo chónaí sa tSruthán. (the locative comes from her cover, so the t before S is hers to copy; the pen checks cónaí for the fada since cónaí is K0474.) Q003 Cá mhéad duine atá sa teaghlach? Tá cúigear sa teaghlach. (pen: teaghlach is K0470, n (m), after sa: the mutation note séimhiú de dhíth and the corrected form sa theaghlach for Ceartúcháin; this is the one form she writes out again before the night closes.) Q004 Cá mhéad deartháir atá agat? Tá deartháir amháin agam. (pen: deartháir is K0749 with its fada; amháin K0070; nothing to mark if both fadas are there.) Q005 Cá mhéad deirfiúr atá agat? Tá beirt deirfiúracha agam, or Níl deirfiúr ar bith agam. (deirfiúr is not on the frequency list, only on the topic list with no gender, so the pen checks the fada by folded match against the topic list and writes nothing about mutation.) Q006 Cá bhfuil tú ar scoil? Tá mé ar scoil in Ardscoil Naomh Pól, an Sruthán. (the school's name in Irish is one string the principal signs off and the app can fill; scoil is K0204.) Q007 Cad é an rang ina bhfuil tú? Tá mé i rang 8C. (pen: nothing.) Ceartúcháin: sa theaghlach, once. Then the stamp in the hand: 28.9.26, Seacht líne, sa theaghlach ceartaithe, maith thú, Sin é anocht. Night two is the four fixed items: 1 Ó chuimhne, Athscríobh Q003 (the line with the correction, box 0, due next night): Tá cúigear sa theaghlach; 2 Focal, a listed word from the next unwritten question Q009 (aois, K0220, n (f)): she writes Tá mé dhá bhliain déag d'aois, tic if aois appears; 3 Foirm, a gap in her own line, Tá cúigear sa ______ (teaghlach); 4 Líne nua, Q009 Cad é an aois thú? Tá mé dhá bhliain déag d'aois. Line grade for Year 8 is one sentence; the item instruction under Líne nua reads Abairt amháin, i do chuid focal féin.
adaptations.firstNightYear12: Identical screens and identical order. The inside cover: Ainm, Rang 12B, Scrúdú Bealtaine 2027, two topic pages ticked by the pupil from the twelve (her real exam choice, say Am saor agus mo ghnáthlá and Mo cheantar), townland and club as before. Then sheet 1a blank with its questions printed on the rules, every question on the sheet at every tier because a Year 12 sheet prints all of them. Then Anocht with the same single item, Q001 to Q007 written together, because the examiner opens with them and a Year 12 also has to have said them before. The difference is the line grade and the pen's full hand. Q001: Aoife Nic Aoidh an t-ainm atá orm agus tá mé sé bliana déag d'aois. Q002: Tá mé i mo chónaí sa tSruthán, sráidbhaile beag cóngarach don Iúr. Q003: Tá seisear sa teaghlach s'againne: mo mhamaí, mo dhaidí, mo bheirt deartháireacha, mo dheirfiúr agus mé féin. Q004: Tá beirt deartháireacha agam agus réitím go maith leo. Q005: Tá deirfiúr amháin agam, Niamh, atá níos óige ná mé. Q006: Tá mé ar scoil in Ardscoil Naomh Pól, an Sruthán, agus is maith liom an scoil mar tá na múinteoirí cairdiúil. Q007: Tá mé i mBliain a Dó Dhéag agus tá mé ag déanamh an TGMO i mbliana. The pen writes the same three checkable things (fada!, a mutation note where the noun's gender is known from a frequency-list row, bheith ag after a bare is maith liom ag) and, from Year 10 up, cad chuige? on an opinion question with no reason word. If this pupil opened the booklet in Year 8, the Q001 rule shows Cara is ainm dom crossed through and dated 2022 above tonight's line; that is the thread made visible. Night two: Ó chuimhne on the most overdue line; Focal from the next question's listed words (Q008 Déan cur síos ort féin: gruaig is not listed, so the picker falls to súil, K0142 n (f)); Foirm cloze on her own sa ______ (teaghlach); Líne nua Q008 in full with an opinion and a reason. The pace line appears on Anocht in print only when unwritten lines on the two pages divided by school nights to Bealtaine exceed one a night; a Year 8 never sees it because the department's June date and a ten-line sheet keep pace under one.
adaptations.whatIsShared: Identical across Years 8 to 12: the register (ruled page, margin rule, italic rubric with English beneath, print instruction per item, biro on the rule, the hand in red in the margin, one action at the foot, grey running foot, no tab bar); the candidate box with its four cells; the six screens (Anocht, An scríbhinn, Líne, Innéacs, Scrúdú béil or Comhrá, An clúdach istigh); the 270 questions as the only questions, with their glosses, openers, follow-up pairs, tense parts and tiers; the twelve Irish page titles and the sheet cuts; the four nightly items in the same order with one live (Ó chuimhne, Focal, Foirm, Líne nua); the pen's rule that it writes only what a teacher could check, capped at three notes, no per-word ticks; the boxes of 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 days with box 0 due next night, a line moving from Athscríobh to Abair é at box 2 and not past box 2 until the sheet has been printed; the Ceartúcháin cap of one form; the close stamp; the printed A4 sheet with the candidate box, a blank rule and a tick box per line for the teacher; Ceartú an mhúinteora typed in as the new key; Mo chuid focal féin and Mo chuid botún; the Script model persisted as JSON in Documents. The vocabulary spine is already shared: the brief fixes listed-word recognition and the article drill on the frequency-list rows with pos n (m) or n (f), 349 nouns with gender, because the topic list's gender is uncleaned, so the KS3 list is the primary spine for every year and the GCSE topic list adds recognition only (fada check, index entry, no gender). One rule is shared but now written down: a line's grade is a property of the pupil's year on the cover, not of the question.

whatDiffers.difference: Two pages fixed by the department (Mé féin agus mo theaghlach; An scoil), not chosen; only tier 1 questions printed on the rules (11 on the first page, 15 on the school page), tier 2 and 3 in grey print at the page foot; sheets of ten; line grade one sentence, instruction Abairt amháin; the pen writes fada! and the mutation note only, never cad chuige? and never bheith ag; Foirm has a second shape for the framework's grammar for meaning: turn your own line into the negative or the question (Imrím peil becomes Ní imrím peil, An imríonn tú peil?), rule-based on the 69 listed verb forms; the third cell reads Comhrá, Meitheamh 2027; Innéacs ordered by frequency band (Na 100 focal is coitianta first) with gender after every noun; Abair é is a self-check only (say the line, hear it back, tic or arís); the pace line never shows.

Two pages fixed by the department (Am saor agus mo ghnáthlá; Mo cheantar), tiers 1 and 2 on the rules; the 42 slash questions with tense alternatives (Q051, Q056, Q063, Q071, Q077 and the travel page Q158 to Q172) are printed as parts a, b and c on separate rules, one tense each, so the same question is answered in three tenses across three nights; line grade one sentence plus a time or place phrase; Foirm adds the tense swap on the pupil's own line (dhéanann to rinne); the pen still withholds cad chuige?; Comhrá, Meitheamh 2027.

Two pages from a department list of six, chosen by the pupil (first choice in the booklet); tiers 1 and 2 on the rules, tier 3 in grey; line grade two sentences with a reason word (mar, mar gheall ar, cionn is, as siocair), instruction Dhá abairt, agus cad chuige; the pen writes cad chuige? on a register opinion question without a reason word, and bheith ag; the third cell reads Comhrá, Meitheamh 2027 and this is the exit conversation for the key stage; Focal may draw from the multi-word phrases (i mbliana, faoin tuath, mar shampla, ar dtús); the cold exam is offered from a finished sheet under the rubric Cúig cheist, gan do scríbhinn os do chomhair.

Two pages chosen by the pupil from all twelve; every tier on the rules, sheets of ten to twenty as the brief cuts them; line grade full answer with an opinion frame and a reason; the full pen; the third cell reads Scrúdú, Bealtaine 2028; the pace line appears when the arithmetic exceeds one line a night; earlier years' drafts on the same question shown crossed through and dated above the live rule.

As Year 11 with Scrúdú, Bealtaine 2027; the two pages are the ones declared for the exam; Priontáil an scríbhinn ar fad as the object the teacher holds in the run-up; Scrúdú béil from every finished sheet with follow-up pairs kept in order; the GCSE-only questions (Q180, Q188, Q229 to Q243, Q254 to Q270) are on the rules for the first time.

adaptations.questionsForYear8: By a curated pass over questions.json, 106 of the 270 can be answered in one present-tense sentence by a beginner using the frequency list plus a handful of personal nouns: Q001 to Q007, Q009 to Q012 (myself and family, 11 of 21); Q022, Q023, Q025 to Q028, Q035 (technology, 7 of 17); Q039 to Q044, Q046 to Q049, Q058, Q063 to Q069, Q072 (free time and routine, 19 of 39); Q078 to Q081, Q085 (festivals, 5 of 9); Q087 to Q091, Q095, Q097, Q100, Q101, Q112, Q115 to Q117 (local area, 13 of 36); Q126, Q129, Q152 (community, 3); Q135, Q137, Q138, Q140, Q142, Q150 (health and issues, 6 of 23); Q158 to Q163, Q165, Q166, Q173 (travel, 9 of 22, past tense but formulaic: Chuaigh mé go Dún na nGall); Q181, Q182, Q184, Q191 to Q198, Q200, Q201, Q204, Q209 (school, 15 of 33); Q213 to Q218 (extra-curricular, 6 of 10); Q223 to Q228, Q244, Q245, Q248, Q249 (money, 10 of 31, mostly Ní bhfaighim or Níl post agam); Q254, Q265 (future, 2 of 17). Of the remaining 164: 44 are shaped by cad chuige, síleann tú, do bharúil, tábhachtach, buntáistí, cé acu is fearr (tier 3); 42 carry a past-tense verb (tier 2 with the 42 slash questions' tense parts); 8 carry a blank (Q093, Q094 unauthored; Q101 to Q106 filled from the townland); and about 30 are GCSE-only in content (Q180 TGMO, Q188 measúnú rialaithe, Q189, Q229 to Q243 taithí oibre and part-time work, Q254 to Q270 Ardléibhéal, BTEC, coláiste, Bliain a Sé) and should never print on a rule below Year 11. On the two Year 8 pages (Mé féin agus mo theaghlach, An scoil) that gives 11 and 15 tier 1 questions, enough for a ten-line sheet and a six-line sheet on each page, with Q008 (Déan cur síos ort féin) and Q203 (Déan cur síos ar ghnáthlá scoile) as the first two-sentence lines at the end of the page. What the KS3 list supplies that the questions do not: gender for 349 nouns (236 m, 113 f), which no question carries and which the mutation note depends on; the 29 prepositional pronouns as a paradigm (agam, agat, liom, leat, orm, ort, dom, duit, aige, aici) which every Tá ... agam answer needs; the 69 verb forms including the negative and interrogative rows (ní bhíonn, An mbíonn, ní dhearna, ní fhaca, ní dheachaigh) and the present habitual forms téann, déanann, tagann, bíonn, which are the framework's grammar for meaning and the raw material for the Year 8 Foirm; the 17 multi-word phrases (mar gheall ar, i mbliana, faoin tuath, cá mhéad, mar shampla, ar dtús, gan dabht) which are the reason and time words the Year 10 line is built on; weather adjectives (scamallach, gaofar, grianmhar, te, fuar) for Q163; numbers one to ten, fiche, céad, míle, and beirt; and the frequency bands themselves, which give the Innéacs an order and the Focal picker a preference (a listed word in the top 500 before one beyond 2000). What the list does not supply and the Year 8 sheet needs: deirfiúr, mamaí, daidí, guthán or fón, éide, cúigear and the other personal numbers above beirt, gorm, glas, buí, donn, suimiúil, leadránach, greannmhar, cineálta, fliuch, eitleán, club, is fearr, dúil, taitin. All but cineálta and fliuch are on the GCSE topic list, gender uncleaned, so they are recognised for the fada and the index but never for mutation until the workbook is cleaned. First-person present forms (imrím, téim, éirím, ithim, amharcaim) are not listed as rows either; the Marker's inflection stop list needs a small table so that Imrím peil counts as the listed imir.
adaptations.frameworkFit: Sound-symbol correspondences: not met. Print carries the spelling but nothing in the app sounds it; Abair é from box 2 is the pupil hearing herself against her own written line, a self-check that shows a dropped syllable but not a wrong vowel. Honest fit only when the Abair Ulster voice is wired in and the question and the line can be heard; until then the framework's phonics strand is the classroom's. High-frequency vocabulary: met. The primary spine is the KS3 list; Focal draws a listed word from the next question with a preference for the lower bands; the Innéacs for Years 8 to 10 is ordered by frequency band with gender after each noun; Mo chuid focal féin holds what is not listed. Grammar for meaning (tense, person, negation, question): met in part. The brief's Foirm covers mutation after preposition and article (meaning-neutral, but examined). For Years 8 to 10 Foirm needs a second shape, the pupil's own line turned negative or interrogative, and in Year 9 the tense swap on the slash questions' parts a, b and c; both are rule-based on the 69 listed verb forms, which carry ní and An rows. Person is met by the prepositional pronoun paradigm in the index and by the question-to-answer swap (agat to agam, tú to mé) the pen could check but the brief does not yet ask it to. Regular recall: met. Ó chuimhne is the first item every night, boxes 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 days, one line never two. Writing from memory: met directly; Athscríobh is writing the pupil's own saved line from memory, marked only on listed words missing. Unprepared speech: met in part. The cold exam from a finished sheet, five questions in print with the sheet face down, recorded, revealed, tic or arís, is unprepared in the sense that the pupil does not know which five; it is not speech to a listener, and the pupil has written every answer before, which is the point of the app but the opposite of unprepared. Honest: the app rehearses prepared speech so that the June conversation can go off the script. A small personal vocabulary: met. Mo chuid focal féin by tap on any word in a line; the cover's townland, school name and club are the personal words the appendix leaves placeholders for. Experience of a real conversation with a fluent speaker: not met by the app and cannot be; met by the date in the candidate box, if the department sets it, and by the printed script the speaker holds. The app's contribution is that the pupil arrives having said every line before.
adaptations.printOnly: The cold exam (Scrúdú béil for 11 and 12, Comhrá for 8 to 10) never depends on a recording of the question. Rubric: Cúig cheist, gan do scríbhinn os do chomhair. From a finished sheet the app picks five written lines at random, follow-up pairs kept in order, and shows each question in print at once, in the print face, on its own page with nothing else; the countdown starts on show; the pupil says the answer into the recorder; on stop the pupil's own line is revealed beneath and the recording plays back automatically (Éist agus amharc); one tap, tic or arís; arís sets the box to 0. The brief's rule that the rubric never reads Mar a bheas sé ar an lá until audio exists stands, and the Audio folder and Q001.m4a to Q270.m4a lines in build step 1 are dropped from the plan. For Year 8 the same screen runs under Comhrá with the countdown kept (it is the only timer in the app and the framework's unprepared speech needs one) but the five questions drawn from tier 1 only. The Abair é item works the same way with no question audio: item 1 shows the question in print with the sheet face down (the line hidden), the pupil says the line from memory, the line is revealed with the recording playing back, tic or arís. Léigh í as a second tap is redundant when print is shown at once and goes. What print cannot do is tell a Year 8 whether she has said the line right; Abair é is a self-check, and the item instruction must say so: Abair í, ansin éist leat féin. When Abair arrives the same two screens gain a play control before the print and the rubric changes; nothing else moves.

adaptations.strategy: Two booklets, one shape. The data structure stays the one the brief chose: one booklet belonging to one pupil, made of pages cut into sheets of ten to twenty numbered lines, a line written in biro a night, marked in the red hand, rewritten from memory, said aloud, printed for the teacher. What changes is what a line answers. For Years 11 and 12 a line answers one of the 270 examiner questions (prompt id Q001 to Q270), exactly as CONCEPT.md has it. For Years 8 to 10 a line completes one authored stem (prompt id S001 onward), a sentence about the pupil built from one grammar frame in the Key Stage 3 appendix (Is mise, Tá ... agam, Tá mé i mo chónaí i, Is maith liom, Imrím, Chuaigh mé go, Rachaidh mé) with one slot that takes a word from the frequency list or from the pupil's own personal vocabulary. The Rang typed on the inside cover (8 to 12) chooses the prompt table silently; the pupil never sees the word stage. A Key Stage 3 line is defined as precisely as a GCSE line: an authored stem in Irish with its English, a slot with a part-of-speech filter, a suggested word chosen by the app from the list, the pupil's completion on the rule, and a pen that checks the same three things plus two the stem makes checkable (the fixed words of the frame present, the slot filled with a listed or personal word). The exam sitting in the candidate box becomes, for Years 8 to 10, the Comhrá: the end-of-year conversation with a fluent speaker that the framework itself requires, with its month. The copybook's stems are tagged with the GCSE question they answer where one exists (96 of the 270 are one-sentence factual questions), so at the first open in Year 11 the pupil's Year 8 sentences appear as dated, crossed-through first drafts under those questions, and the script's first sheet is already half written. Where the strategy strains: phonics cannot be met in print; unprepared speech is only partly met; the real conversation is the school's to hold, not the app's; Year 10 sits awkwardly between stems and questions and is given the 96 factual questions as its own page.
adaptations.threadForYear8: For a Year 8 the script is a copybook of sentences about herself, page by page (Mé féin, Mo theaghlach, Mo theach agus mo cheantar, An scoil), each page cut into sheets of ten to twenty lines, each line an Irish stem printed on the rule (Tá ... deartháir agam, I have ... brothers) that she completes in biro in her own words, marked in the Principal's red hand for fadas, mutation after a preposition and the article on the 362 nouns whose gender the list gives, and a missing frame word (agam de dhíth), rewritten from memory on later nights and said aloud once it has been right twice, printed for the teacher who corrects the rest. What fills is the sheet: twelve lines in a fortnight, Críochnaithe written across it in the hand, then the page, then the four pages of Year 8 by Easter. The candidate box says Ainm, Rang 8B, Comhrá Meitheamh 2027 and Líne 5 de 12: no exam, but a real date, the June conversation with a fluent speaker that the framework requires and the department sets, at which she will be asked about herself and will have nothing to say for the first time. A twelve-year-old opens it tomorrow because tonight's page is one sentence about her own dog, the mark comes the second she writes it, the sheet is visibly two lines from full, and the correction from last night (sa charr) is sitting in red beside the line that retests it.

Page 9, An comhrá: the 96 factual one-sentence questions from questions.json become the lines, printed on the rules as questions exactly as the Year 11 script does, so a Year 10 writes answers to the examiner's own simple questions before ever seeing the word scrúdú. Frames from pages 1 to 8 are offered as the word bank's first row. Foirm becomes the GCSE cloze (preposition plus article plus noun blanked in the pupil's own line) alongside the tense turn. Focal as GCSE: a listed word from the next question's own words in the pupil's own sentence. Candidate box cell 3: Scrúdú béil with the month if the department sets a Year 10 oral, else Comhrá. The 96 lines migrate at Year 11 as first drafts under the same question ids.

CONCEPT.md as written: two topic pages ticked from twelve, the 270 questions, openers, Foirm cloze, cad chuige? on opinion questions, bheith ag, Scrúdú Bealtaine 2028 in the box. Plus: any copybook line whose stem or question id matches appears as a dated crossed-through first draft (Bliain 8, Bliain 10) under its question on first open, and the pupil's personal words carry over. Pace line arithmetic runs from the first open.

As Year 11 with Scrúdú Bealtaine 2027; the pace line is the one thing likelier to surface, since two pages of about 60 lines against about 150 school nights leaves no slack for a late start; Scrúdú béil is offered from the first finished sheet and is the only place with a countdown.

risks: The Comhrá may not exist. If the department does not hold an end-of-year conversation with a fluent speaker for Years 8 to 10, the third cell of a Year 8's candidate box is a promise the school is not keeping, and the copybook has no date at all; the framework requires the experience, so the school must find the speaker regardless, but the app cannot make it happen.

Phonics is simply not met until Abair, and the Key Stage 3 framework puts it first. A copybook that never voices a word is honest but a Year 8 who cannot read Irish aloud will not be helped to by print, and the Abair é recording with no check may rehearse a wrong sound for three years.

Stems are authored content in a way the questions are not. About 65 stems with three or five forms each is 200 strings to write in Ulster Irish and sign off, and a wrong paradigm form in the table marks a right line wrong in the Principal's hand. The sign-off is on the critical path for Year 8, which starts before Year 11 needs anything.

A stem is not a question. The sheet reads as a paragraph about the pupil only if the stems are ordered with care; done badly it is a grammar drill in a copybook's clothes, which the panel already rejected, and a Year 8 will feel the difference inside a week.

The Key Stage 3 list is a frequency list plus 96 topic words, with real gaps for a Year 8 (colours, uniform, drink, fruit, boy, sick, doctor, phone), so the slot suggestion will often be empty or odd and the pupil will write unlisted words the pen cannot see; the tap-to-add personal vocabulary absorbs this but the Innéacs will fill with words that carry no gender.

Foirm's paradigm turn is only as good as the stored forms and the folded token match; a pupil who writes a correct but different question (Cá mhéad deartháir atá agat?) is marked against the stored one. The pen must write nothing when the line contains the stored form's key tokens in any order, and the README must say so.

Year 10 is the seam. The 96 factual questions as a page give it a purpose, but a Year 10 who reaches page 9 in October has eight months of questions with no opinion frames and no reason words, and the June cell may say Comhrá when the department holds nothing.

Migration into the Year 11 script carries Year 8 sentences that were never corrected by a teacher; a wrong line written in Year 8, printed but never marked on paper, becomes the crossed-through draft the Year 11 answer grows from. The printed sheet's tick box is the only defence and depends on teachers marking paper.

Five years on one device. The copybook to script continuity is the whole point of one booklet for the school, and the PoC keeps everything in Documents on one phone; without iCloud or a school account the thread breaks at the first lost phone, most likely between Year 9 and Year 10.

Unprepared speech remains the framework's word for something the booklet only half does; an inspector reading the copybook as rote answers is a risk the department should answer with the Comhrá and the printed sheet, not the app.

adaptations.strategy: The conversation, not the exam. The thread becomes: one pupil's own script of what they will say in their next conversation in Irish with a fluent speaker. The 270 questions are kept as the data (they are the questions fluent speakers ask a learner: name, home, family, school, free time, and later opinion), but the date in the candidate box is the next conversation, not an exam sitting. The school stages a ladder of conversations that every year already has or can have: Year 8, a Year 12 partner and then a visiting speaker; Year 9, a visitor or the Gaeltacht; Year 10, a visitor or a June scrúdú béil if the department sets one; Year 11, the mock with the teacher; Year 12, the examiner. Each is a row on the inside cover (partner, date); the box shows the next one. Everything else in CONCEPT.md stands: the same six screens, the four nightly items, the red hand, the Leitner boxes, the printed sheet with a rule and tick box per line. The year only gates which questions are open (a tier field) and which tense of a slash question is shown (the part field the brief already plans). Print is the natural medium for this: the printed sheet becomes the conversation card, the questions on it are read aloud by the partner, so the first voice a Year 8 hears asking the questions is a fluent human one, which is what the Key Stage 3 framework asks for and what the missing audio cannot supply anyway. Where it strains: the reframe is fully true for the roughly 128 factual present-tense questions and Years 8 to 10; for the opinion and description questions of Years 11 and 12 (Cad iad na buntáistí, An é do bharúil) it is honestly the examiner's register, and the Year 12 box should keep the word scrúdaitheoir. The reframe also depends on the department setting a real date per class each half term; without that a Year 8's box reads gan dáta go fóill and the thread is as empty as the brief's was.

adaptations.frameworkFit: Sound-symbol correspondences: not met inside the app while there is no audio, and it should not be claimed. Half of it is possible in print: Abair é has the pupil read their own line aloud, record it and hear it back against the revealed print, which is the read-aloud direction only, judged by the pupil alone; the hear-and-type direction and any correction of pronunciation wait for Abair, and the fluent partner in the conversation is the only corrector until then. The repository holds no phonics rows. High-frequency vocabulary: met, through Focal drawing listed words from the next question, the Innéacs listing only words already in a line with gender, and the printed sheet; 797 usable rows once the 29 legend rows are dropped, 362 gendered nouns for the article drill. Honest limit: the top 100 are function words that Focal excludes by part of speech, so they are learned by writing lines, not drilled. Grammar for meaning (tense, person, negation, question): met in part by Foirm on the pupil's own line (article and mutation, prepositional pronoun cloze), by the part field opening present in Year 8, past in Year 9 and future in Year 10, and by negation arising naturally (Níl deirfiúr ar bith agam); question forms are not met by the exam script at all, since the candidate never asks, and the reframe adds the Ceist ar ais line to meet it. Regular recall: met, the Ó chuimhne item every night and boxes of 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 days. Writing from memory: met, Athscríobh ó chuimhne with the pen marking only listed words missing from the saved line. Unprepared speech: not met inside the app, and the whole point of the script is that nothing is said for the first time; the rehearsal screen draws from written lines and is prepared by design. judgements.lens: A 12-year-old in Year 8 at St Paul's, three weeks into Irish, never sat an exam, owns a phone. Two questions only: do I understand what this booklet is for, and does it feel like mine.

scores.strategy: One booklet for the whole school, graded lines
scores.bestIdea: A line's grade is a property of the year on the cover, not of the question (Abairt amháin in Year 8; Dhá abairt, agus cad chuige in Year 10; Freagra iomlán in Year 12), so the same Q004 rule carries Tá deartháir amháin agam in 2026 crossed through under a full Year 12 answer in 2030. That one sentence is the whole-school thread in a form a pupil can state, and it costs one field.
scores.weakestPoint: To a 12-year-old the booklet is still visibly someone else's exam script: the questions on the rules are the examiner's, the page foot carries grey questions about TGMO and taithí oibre she cannot read, and the date in the box is nine months away with a person she cannot picture. 'Comhrá, Meitheamh 2027' is a label on a promise, not a reason to open it tomorrow. The tier pass also has holes: cúigear and the other personal numbers are on the list (K0748 etc.), so the 'gap' list is padded, while cionn is, which the Year 10 line is supposedly built on, is not on the list at all.

scores.strategy: Two booklets, one shape (stems for Years 8 to 10, questions for 11 and 12)
scores.bestIdea: Foirm as a turn on the pupil's own line: Scríobh í mar cheist, Scríobh í sa diúltach, mar a bhí inné, diagnosed by rule against the 69 listed verb rows that already carry ní and An forms (K0138 ní bhíonn, K0205 an mbíonn, K0723 ní dheachaigh). It is the only one of the three that meets the framework's grammar for meaning directly, and turning my own sentence into a question is something a Year 8 can do and enjoy on night two.
scores.weakestPoint: It is two apps in one, and a 12-year-old feels it: a stem (Tá ___ deartháir agam) is the app's sentence with my word in it, not my line, so the copybook reads as a worksheet however carefully the stems are ordered, and the writers admit it ('a grammar drill in a copybook's clothes', which the panel already rejected). Year 10 is a seam nobody can state in one sentence. And about 65 stems with three to five forms each, 200 strings in Ulster Irish, sit on the principal's critical path before a single Year 8 can start, ahead of everything Year 11 needs; a wrong paradigm form in that table marks a right line wrong in his hand.

scores.bestIdea: The printed sheet as the conversation card, read aloud by a named fluent human (a Year 12 partner in three weeks, then a visitor before Christmas), with a tick box the partner fills and one Ceist ar ais line per sheet so the Year 8 asks a question back. It turns the missing audio into a feature (the first voice to ask the questions is a real one), gives the framework's real conversation a place in the app's data, and gives a 12-year-old the one thing that makes a booklet hers: a person who is going to ask her these exact questions on a date she can count down to.
scores.weakestPoint: The whole thread rests on a timetable commitment the app cannot make. If the department does not stage a conversation per class each half term and find the partners, the box reads gan dáta go fóill and a Year 8 is holding an empty promise, exactly the fault the rejected narrowing had. Year 12 partners cost Irish lessons and supervision. The relabelling to Comhrá also softens the Year 12 cover (the questions 'Irish speakers ask you' is not true of Cad iad na buntáistí), and the data pass is careless: it lists personal numerals and deirfiúr as absent when triúr to deichniúr are listed and deirfiúir sits at K0750, and claims go raibh maith agat is in the GCSE Beannachtaí group when it is in neither list.

judgements.rationale: Judged as a Year 8 three weeks in, the question is not which adaptation is most complete but which one I would understand and open tomorrow. Adaptation 3 is the only one where I can say in one sentence what the booklet is for (what I will say to the Year 12 who is going to ask me these questions on 14 Samhain) and the only one where the object I carry (the printed card with my lines and their tick boxes) is mine and is used by a real person. It scores 5 on one thread because every year from 8 to 12 states the same idea and the year only changes the partner, and it keeps the Year 12 script almost intact (4, not 5, because the cover text and box label soften the examiner's register for a Year 12 in spring). It loses on buildability (3) because the conversation rows, the greeting lines and the comhrá calendar are not in the repository and the staging is the school's, not the app's, and its weakest point is fatal if the department will not set dates: the thread is then as empty as the one the principal rejected. Adaptation 1 (19) is the safest to build and the truest to the winning concept, and its rule that the line grade follows the year on the cover should be grafted into the winner, but to a 12-year-old it is a Year 12's exam script handed down, with grey exam questions at the foot and a June date nine months off; it also miscounts the vocabulary gaps (personal numbers are listed, cionn is is not). Adaptation 2 (16) meets the framework best on grammar for meaning and reads the data most accurately (the 96 Thar 2000 rows, the deirfiúir misspelling, the personal numbers), and its Foirm turn on the pupil's own line should be grafted, but it is two apps with a seam at Year 10, the stem is the app's sentence not the pupil's, and 200 authored strings sit on the principal's sign-off path before any Year 8 can start. Synthesis: take 3 as the thread, 1's graded line and grey-foot tiering as the mechanism, 2's Foirm turn and cover placeholders as the framework's grammar and personal vocabulary, and make the department's conversation calendar the first decision only Dáithí can make, because without it none of the three holds for Year 8.

judgements.lens: Head of Irish: one scheme across Years 8 to 12 that meets the Key Stage 3 framework from 2028 and still gets Year 12 through the speaking exam. Claims each strategy makes about the data were checked; where a strategy misreads the data the score is docked, because the pen only works on what the data holds.

scores.strategy: One booklet for the whole school, graded lines
scores.bestIdea: A line's grade is a property of the year on the cover, not of the question: one sentence in Year 8, two with a reason word in Year 10, a full answer with an opinion in Year 12, the same 270 questions on every cover, the untiered ones in grey print at the foot of the sheet as not yet asked, and the Year 8 draft left crossed through and dated under the Year 12 line. It needs no new screen and no new prompt table; the Líne screen already keeps dated drafts.
scores.weakestPoint: Its own first night has the pen writing a wrong correction in the Principal's hand: sa teaghlach is right (sa does not lenite d, t or s; the question Q003 itself reads sa teaghlach), yet the strategy has the pen write séimhiú de dhíth and make sa theaghlach the one form Cara writes out again. In a register whose whole claim is that the pen writes only what a teacher could check, night one would teach a Year 8 an error. It also misreads the list (cúigear K0748, triúr K0395, ceathrar, seachtar K0728, deichniúr K0780 and gruaig K0755 are all present) and its tier 1 list contains Q254 and Q265 while its gcseOnly flag also names them.

scores.bestIdea: The stored paradigm behind a line: negative, question with the person shifted (agam to agat), past and future, so Foirm turns the pupil's own sentence by rule and the pen can write agat, ní agam. That is the framework's grammar for meaning (tense, person, negation, question) done inside the pupil's own writing rather than in a drill, and it can be grafted onto a question-keyed line just as well as a stem. Its reading of the list is the most accurate of the three (cúigear to deichniúr present, deirfiúir misspelt at K0750, gaol as n (mpl), the 96 Thar 2000 rows as the Year 8 topic words).
scores.weakestPoint: It is two half-schemes by construction: a Year 8 completes stems S001 onward, a Year 11 answers questions Q001 onward, and Year 10 is given a third thing (the 96 factual questions as a page) to paper the seam. The pupil cannot state one idea that covers both. Some 65 stems with three to five forms each, about 200 strings, must be authored and signed off by the principal before September of Year 8, none of which exists in the repository today, and the 62-row phonics table it bundles is not in the repository either. A wrongly stored paradigm form marks a right line wrong in the Principal's hand.

scores.bestIdea: The printed sheet as the conversation card: the questions in print on the left for a fluent partner (a Year 12 pupil, a visitor, the teacher, the examiner) to read aloud and tick, so the first voice a Year 8 hears asking the questions is a fluent human one. It is the only strategy that turns ruling 2 (no audio until Abair) into a feature rather than a gap, and Ceist ar ais (the pupil flips one question on the sheet to ask the partner) is the only proposal that meets the framework's question forms at all, since an exam candidate never asks.
scores.weakestPoint: The thread is a timetable the school does not have: a real date per class each half term and Year 12 partners taken out of Irish lessons under supervision. Without it the Year 8 box reads gan dáta go fóill and the strategy admits the thread is then as empty as the rejected narrowing. Its Year 8 tier list also breaks its own gate: Q083, Q183 and Q185 carry cad chuige and Q205 asks is mó a thaitníonn, yet all sit in its tier 8, while it claims cad chuige never fires below Year 10. judgements.winner: One booklet for the whole school, graded lines
judgements.rationale: Strategy 1 wins because it is the only one that is one scheme rather than two: one booklet, one set of 270 questions, one first night (Q001 to Q007 written together) for every year, and a single rule a pupil can state (the line gets longer as you get older, the question does not change). Year 12 is untouched, which matters more than anything else in a department that has to sit the exam every May. Strategy 3 is close and its two grafts are not optional: the printed sheet must double as the conversation card read aloud by a fluent partner, since that is the only honest answer to a print-only app and to the framework's real conversation, and Ceist ar ais must be adopted once per sheet, since nothing else in any strategy produces a question form from the pupil. Strategy 2's stored paradigm (negative, question with person shifted, past, future) should replace strategy 1's looser Foirm variant; it can key off a question-answer line as easily as a stem. Strategy 2 as a whole is rejected on the head of Irish's own criterion: two prompt tables with a Year 10 seam is two half-schemes, and 200 unsigned strings sit on the critical path before a Year 8 opens the app. Three corrections bind the synthesis regardless of winner. First, sa does not lenite d, t or s: the Mutate.prepArticle rule in CONCEPT.md step 4 needs that exception written in, or the pen will do on night one exactly what strategy 1's example shows. Second, the personal numerals are on the list (triúr K0395, cúigear K0748, seachtar K0728, deichniúr K0780, ceathrar and seisear too) and so is gruaig K0755; the real gaps are deirfiúr (listed only as deirfiúir), mamaí, daidí, guthán, éide, the colours gorm, glas, buí, donn, suimiúil, greannmhar, leadránach, club, eitleán, go raibh maith agat, and the first-person verb forms; the GCSE list carries most of these but with 827 rows marked m and none f, so it can be used for the fada and the index but never for mutation. Third, every tier count offered (106, 96, 128) is a reader's guess and the three disagree; the tier field is a judgement the principal signs off question by question, with the gcseOnly set (Q180, Q188, Q189, Q229 to Q243, Q254 to Q270) kept off every rule below Year 11. On the framework, all three are honest that sound-symbol correspondences are not met until Abair and that the real conversation is the school's to hold, not the app's; the June Comhrá date in the candidate box is therefore a department obligation to be ruled on, and if it is not set the cell must carry the sheet's print date rather than a promise.

judgements.rationale: Judged against the data as it exists: questions.json has 270 rows with id, ga, topic and context only (no tier, part, gloss or register yet); 42 slash rows, 8 blanks, 79 An/Ar/Nach rows, 44 opinion-shaped rows, about 28 past-tense rows by verb; vocab.json carries 826 ks3 rows in seven frequency groups (76, 95, 117, 177, 236, 96 Thar 2000, 29 legend rows with empty pos), 246 m and 116 f gendered rows, 29 pppn, 69 v, 17 mwp, and it does hold cúigear, triúr, ceathrar, deirfiúir (misspelt, K0750), teaghlach, deartháir, aois, but not mamaí, daidí, guthán, éide, gorm, glas, suimiúil, greannmhar, club or cionn is. All three strategies need the same tier pass on the 270 signed off by the principal and all three are honest that phonics and the real conversation are outside the app. Strategy 2 loses on the only criterion this lens weights heaviest: a stem table and a question table are two products, the Year 10 seam is admitted, and 200 authored strings sit ahead of Year 8's first night. Strategies 1 and 3 keep one file, one set of 270 questions, the same six screens and the same four-item night. Strategy 1 is the safer build (smallest delta from the brief, tier plus gcseOnly plus a lineGrade derived from yearGroup) and it still wins Year 12 untouched, but its Year 8 thread is the exam object with the exam removed: a date nine months off, greyed examiner questions at the page foot, and a booklet whose cover text still has to be rewritten by year. Strategy 3 wins because the object means the same thing on every cover: what I will say in my next conversation with a fluent speaker, with the examiner as the last rung of a ladder rather than the point of the booklet, and because it makes print-only the design rather than a limitation (the card the partner reads from). It wins narrowly and conditionally: the department must commit to a staged conversation per class per half term, and the Year 12 cell should keep Scrúdú as its label at the cost of one conditional. Graft from Strategy 1 the line grade as a property of the year on the cover, which Strategy 3 lacks (a Year 12 answering Q001 in one sentence would pass its pen), and the earlier draft crossed through and dated above the later line; graft from Strategy 2 the Foirm paradigm turn on the pupil's own line for the framework's negation and question forms, and its cleaner reading of the vocabulary data (fix deirfiúir to deirfiúr at K0750 rather than adding a supplement row). Both remaining strategies should correct their claims that personal numbers and deirfiúr are absent from the KS3 list, and Strategy 1 should drop the K0142 súil reference.

brief.brief:
## What it is for

Write what you will say in your next conversation in Irish, one line a night, until nothing is new.

After twenty school nights: twenty lines in biro on two pages, the first sheet finished, each line rewritten from memory and said aloud, one printed sheet back from the teacher with a correction typed in.

## The thread

The script. One booklet belonging to one pupil from Year 8 to the exam in Year 12, the data structure and not a skin: topic pages cut into sheets of numbered lines; a line is the pupil's own answer to one of the 270 questions, in biro, marked in the Principal's red hand for what a machine can check, printed for the teacher who corrects the rest, rewritten and said from memory until it is theirs. The questions are those a fluent speaker asks a learner; the examiner is the last of them.

Two rules hold it for every year. The question is the same on every cover; the line's grade follows the year on the cover: one sentence in Year 8, two with a reason word in Year 10, a full answer with an opinion in Year 12. The date on the cover, carried on every screen in the candidate box (Ainm, Rang, the date cell, Líne 5 de 11, never a score), is the next conversation with a fluent speaker (teacher, Year 12 partner, visitor; for Years 11 and 12 the examiner), whose card is the printed sheet. A Year 8 line stays under the Year 12 answer, crossed through and dated. The italic rubric with its English beneath is the only heading; one action at the foot; no tab bar.

## First open

The inside cover: Ainm, Rang (8 to 12), the next conversation from the board or the exam month, two topic pages (fixed by the department for Years 8 and 9, from its six in Year 10, from twelve in 11 and 12), townland as said after Tá mé i mo chónaí, club as said after Imrím le, the school's name in Irish. Then the first sheet, blank, its questions on the rules. The cover's text is permanent.

Irish: Seo do scríbhinn féin. Ar na leathanaigh seo tá na ceisteanna a chuirfeas cainteoir Gaeilge ort sa chomhrá, agus do chuid freagraí féin orthu. Achan oíche: líne amháin nua i do chuid focal féin, agus líne a scríobh tú cheana, ó chuimhne. Ceartóidh an peann dearg na fadaí, an séimhiú agus an t-urú; is í an aip a mharcálann, i lámh an Phríomhoide. Do mhúinteoir a cheartóidh an chuid eile, ón leathanach a phriontálann tú. Faoin chéad chomhrá eile ní bheidh rud ar bith le rá agat den chéad uair.

English beneath, line for line.

## Home

No home apart from the work: the app opens on Anocht. Every night the rubric reads Do chomhrá, scríofa agat roimh ré, English beneath. Night one, every year: the seven one-sentence questions Q001 to Q007, written together.

## The screens

**1. Anocht.** Four items, fixed order, one live. 1 Ó chuimhne, the most overdue line: in box 0 or 1 Athscríobh from memory, marked only on listed words missing; from box 2 Abair é, said with the line hidden, played back against it. 2 Focal: a word missed in item 1, else a listed word from the next question, in the pupil's own sentence. 3 Foirm: the pupil's own line turned by rule: a gap where preposition and article meet a noun of known gender, sa ______ (carr); or the line made negative, made a question with the person shifted, or from Year 9 put in another tense, checked against the 69 listed verb forms. 4 Líne nua: the next question at the year's tier; once per sheet Ceist ar ais instead, one printed question turned round to ask the partner. The pen writes at most three things: fada!; a mutation note where a frequency-list row gives the noun's gender, never on d, t or s; from Year 10, cad chuige? on an opinion question without a reason word and bheith ag after a bare is maith liom ag. Opener in grey after twenty seconds; Fág go fóill skips; Ceartúcháin one form; the stamp: date, one kind line, Sin é anocht.

**2. An scríbhinn.** Rubric: Gach a ndéarfaidh tú sa chomhrá. The two pages and their sheets, the rest grey; on a sheet's rules only questions at the year's tier, the rest in grey at its foot, not yet asked; Críochnaithe across a finished sheet; Priontáil an leathanach.

**3. Líne.** Rubric: the question. Drafts crossed through and dated, earlier years' among them, recordings, word bank, Athscríobh ó chuimhne, Ceartú an mhúinteora typed in as the key.

**4. Innéacs.** Rubric: Na focail atá i do scríbhinn. Words already in a line, by sheet, gender where known, line reference; then Mo chuid focal féin and Mo chuid botún.

**5. Comhrá gan scríbhinn, Scrúdú béil for 11 and 12.** Rubric: Cúig cheist, gan do scríbhinn os do chomhair; Trí cheist in Year 8. From a finished sheet, pairs in sequence, each question in print at once, the only countdown, record, reveal, playback, tic or arís. Abair later adds a play control.

**6. An clúdach istigh.** Rubric: Cé thú féin agus cá huair a bheas an chéad chomhrá eile. The details, the conversation rows over five years, the text, Priontáil an scríbhinn ar fad, Glan.

## The years

Shared: the screens, the items and their order, the 270 questions and twelve pages, the pen, the boxes of 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 days, the printed card, the Key Stage 3 frequency list as the spine for recognition and gender (349 nouns), the topic list for recognition only (it marks no feminine), one Script file across five years.

What differs, and only this:

- Year 8: two pages fixed by the department; tier 1 questions only on the rules (95 by a first pass); sheets of ten; Abairt amháin; the present part of the six tense questions; the pen writes fada! and the mutation note only; no pace line.
- Year 9: pages fixed; tier 2 (tense parts, descriptions, the travel page); sheets of twelve; one sentence with a time or place phrase; Foirm adds the tense turn.
- Year 10: two pages from the department's six; tier 3, the 33 opinion or reason questions; Dhá abairt, agus cad chuige; cad chuige? and bheith ag begin.
- Year 11: two pages from twelve; every tier and the 36 gcseOnly questions, never on a rule below Year 11; Freagra iomlán; sheets of ten to twenty; Scrúdú, Bealtaine 2028; the pace line above one line a night.
- Year 12: as Year 11 with Bealtaine 2027; Priontáil an scríbhinn ar fad for the teacher.

## A school night in five minutes, twice

Caoimhe, 8B, sheet 1a, Líne 8 de 10, Comhrá: Bliain 12, 14 Samhain. Item 1, Athscríobh 1a.4, Cá mhéad deartháir atá agat?: amháin left out; amháin de dhíth. Item 2: deartháir in her own sentence; dearthair, fada!. Item 3, her own 1a.4, Scríobh í mar cheist: An bhfuil deartháir agam?; agat, ní agam. Item 4, Cad é an caitheamh aimsire is fearr leat?: Is maith liom peil. Ceartúcháin: deartháir once. Stamp: 6.10.26, deartháir ceartaithe, maith thú, Sin é anocht.

Aoife, 11B, sheet 1b, Líne 5 de 11, Scrúdú: Bealtaine 2028. Item 1, Athscríobh 1a.4: amháin de dhíth. Item 2: amháin in her own sentence, tic. Item 3, sa ______ (carr) from her own 1a.2: carr; charr above, séimhiú de dhíth. Item 4, Cad é mar a réitíonn tú le do chlann?: Réitím go maith le mo chlann. Is maith liom ag caint le mo mhamaí mar tá sí greannmhar. The pen writes bheith ag caint. Ceartúcháin: sa charr once. Stamp: sa charr ceartaithe. Under her 1a.4, Tá deartháir amháin agam, crossed through, 2023.

## The exam-script register, what it must do

The test for every screen: could it be printed and handed to a teacher as a page of a candidate's script, or to the partner as the card for the conversation. The pen writes only what a teacher could check; the printed sheet carries the question, a blank rule and a tick box per line.

## For a pupil with ADHD

Progress is an object that fills inside a fortnight: a sheet, Críochnaithe across it. The same four items in the same order every night, one live; the queue never shown. Marking is instant; one wrong form is written out again before the night closes. No streak, no timer except the cold exam.

## What comes out of the current build

The TabView; HomeView's statistics and streak; the score slot in ExamHeader; the Aonad labels; GrammarView; SettingsView's Form and stage picker; intervals 0, 1, 3, 7, 14, 30; per-word ticks; the Audio folder; the narrowing to Years 11 and 12; the name Cuimhne.

## What has to be true before it can be built

Data: a twelve-row topic table with Irish page titles and sheet cuts; the 270 questions each with gloss, tier (1 factual, 2 tense or description, 3 opinion or reason), gcseOnly flag, register, follow-up pair and opener; the six tense questions cut into parts, the other slashes settled, Q093 and Q094 authored; the department's pages for Years 8 to 10 and a conversation date per class; the school's name in Irish; a first-person verb table so Imrím folds to imir; every Irish string signed off by the Principal. Audio: none until Abair. Model answers: none. One booklet, Years 8 to 12; phonics and the real conversation are the classroom's.
